title: Measures of Anchoring in Estimation Tasks

source.title: Measures of Anchoring in Estimation Tasks

studies.title: Experiment · Estimates with and without anchors

fields.label: Question
fields.value: How large is anchoring in numerical estimates, and can one compare its size across very different questions?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: One questionnaire study with an unanchored calibration sample and two anchored groups, followed by analyses of anchor judgments and confidence.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: High and low anchors both moved numerical estimates. High anchors also shifted the initial comparison itself, and high confidence did not eliminate the effect.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: The study asks whether anchors move estimates toward the presented value and whether this differs with initial anchor judgments and self-reported confidence.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: The descriptive anchoring index and the percentile comparison are different measures. Confidence is self-reported, and the comparisons do not uniquely identify the mechanism behind anchoring.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: 156 Berkeley students answered questions about 15 quantities. The calibration group (53) made unanchored estimates. For the other 103, the 15th or 85th calibration percentile supplied the anchor for each question. People first compared the quantity with the anchor, then estimated it and rated confidence.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: The mean question-level anchoring index was 0.49. Median transformed estimates were at the 76th calibration percentile for high anchors and 36th for low anchors.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Compare the frequency of estimates outside the anchors with calibration predictions. Analyze confidence alongside the movement of estimates.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: High anchors were judged too low on 27% of occasions and low anchors too high on 14%. The initial comparison itself could already be biased. Anchoring was smaller, but still present, among the most confident estimates (mean index 0.28 versus 0.49 overall).
